explanations.explanation: This neuron is a structural‐boundary detector – it spikes on the blank/newline plus the very first token of a new section or header (titles, headings, docket numbers, metadata lines, etc.). It marks the start of a distinct document block.

This neuron isn’t picking out any semantic theme or part of speech—instead it is essentially a one‐hot detector for a small, idiosyncratic set of BPE subword tokens (e.g. “er,” “hard,” “Script,” “150,” “IG,” “X,” “Tr,” “ơ,” “j,” etc.). It fires whenever one of those exact subword pieces appears, regardless of the bigger context.

This neuron is basically a subword-stem detector: it lights up on the interior sequences of multi-syllable content words (roots or affixes like “resiz-,” “optim-,” “-able,” “twist-/detwist-,” “paniculata,” etc.), especially in domain-specific or technical vocabulary.

This neuron is picking up on “namespace” or “dotted‐name” tokens – i.e. the individual subwords you see in hierarchical identifiers (domain names, Python module imports/attributes, JSON/PSScript property keys, config fields, etc.).

This feature fires on adjectival or determinative words that single out or specify one element (or subset) within a larger set or spatial arrangement—e.g. “remaining,” “single,” “specific,” “other,” “each,” “neighboring,” “overlying,” etc.
This feature is simply picking up the BPE piece “V” – i.e. the initial, capital‐letter V that begins words like Viva, Vaccines, Viking, Vintage, Video, Villa, Vascular, etc.

This feature lights up on discourse-modulating words—mainly adverbs, adjectives or participles—that introduce emphasis, contrast, hedging or speaker stance (e.g. “intentionally,” “very,” “though,” “while,” “considering,” “commonly,” etc.).

This feature fires on high-information content words—mostly nouns and verbs that name the central function, process or topic in a technical or scientific passage (e.g. impact, gauges, photosynthesis, catalyze, draw, induce)—effectively flagging the key actions or themes in the text.

explanations.explanation: This feature fires on the final period that ends a scientific paper’s title, effectively marking the title–abstract boundary.

This feature fires on the main noun-head of a clause—the actor, role or key component that the sentence is about (e.g. “governor,” “perpetrator,” “fellow,” “unit,” “groom,” “experts,” “subject,” “receiving,” “outing,” etc.). It thus marks the central entity or agentive noun around which each statement pivots.
